overview.label: 01 — OVERVIEW
overview.heading: Project Background & Motivation
overview.body:
In July 2023, I joined the AAPD UI Bootcamp — an intensive program focused on elevating designers' UI design and UX decision-making skills. Over two weeks, I worked with four designers from different industries to complete this project, winning the Gold Award in a team competition among 200+ participants.

The timing of this project was special: ChatGPT had launched just six months prior, and Duolingo along with many global platforms released their own AI features around the same time in 2023. We chose an AI course learning platform based on our read of market trends — AI-assisted learning was at the tipping point of moving from concept to product.
overview.calloutTitle: The market later validated this judgment
overview.calloutBody: The global AI education market is projected to grow from $5.88B in 2024 to $32.27B by 2030 (CAGR 31.2%). Khan Academy's AI tutor Khanmigo grew from 68K users to over 1.4 million.
overview.calloutSource: — Grand View Research, 2025; Khan Academy Official Data
overview.imageCaption: Platform overview — Homepage, course detail, and AI tutor

myRole.label: 02 — MY ROLE
myRole.heading: Leading visual direction & engineering handoff
myRole.intro: In two intense weeks, I was primarily responsible for two things:
myRole.card1Title: Led the overall product design direction
myRole.card1Body: From moodboard to final visual language, including the color system, typography standards, and proposing and leading the product's style direction.
myRole.card2Body: UI Flow connections, interaction state annotations for every screen, and component behavior specifications. This is a core competency from my previous work experience, enabling rapid integration within limited time.
myRole.collab: Other collaborative areas included competitive analysis, component design and iteration, and interface design — completed through team division of work.

research.label: 03 — RESEARCH
research.heading: From market observation to pain point synthesis
research.body: We observed AI courses proliferating across major learning platforms as a trending new category. Through interviewing AI learners and competitive analysis, we understood the product landscape and market, using the CIRCLES framework and 5W1H to define product positioning.
research.img1Caption: AI course category trends across platforms
research.fiveW1H_who1: AI beginners and cross-disciplinary learners (want to learn AI but don't know where to start)
research.fiveW1H_who2: Instructors across fields (want to share AI tool expertise)
research.fiveW1H_what1: An online learning platform focused on AI courses, with a 'site-wide companion AI tutor' as core differentiator
research.fiveW1H_when1: July 2023 — just 6 months after ChatGPT launched, AI education shifting from concept to product
research.fiveW1H_when2: AI courses booming across platforms, but no one had nailed the 'AI-assisted learning experience' itself
research.fiveW1H_where1: Browsing the homepage (don't know what to learn → AI helps find courses)
research.fiveW1H_where2: Hesitating on course pages (unsure if it's right → AI answers instantly)
research.fiveW1H_where3: During learning (stuck on a concept → AI acts as a tutor)
research.fiveW1H_why1: Three core pain points: can't find the right course, uncertainty before purchase, lack of companionship while learning
research.fiveW1H_how1: Floating Chat Panel (site-wide), with three contextual Tabs (Find Courses / Course Q&A / Learning Assistant) to reduce blank canvas cognitive load
research.pain1Body: Overwhelmed by the volume of AI courses with no clear starting point. Traditional category filters can't understand natural language needs.
research.pain2Body: Still uncertain after reading course descriptions — is the difficulty right for me? What prerequisites do I need? No immediate answers available.
research.pain3Body: When stuck on a concept, the only options are rewatching videos or searching on your own — missing a 'just ask and understand' tutor role.

goal.label: 04 — GOAL
goal.heading: Defining scope through User Stories
goal.story1: I want to browse the latest and trending courses on the homepage to understand what the platform offers
goal.story2: I want to view course details, instructor bio, and syllabus on the course page to judge if it's right for me
goal.story3: I want to quickly find courses matching my needs through search
goal.pos1Highlight: platform focused on exploring and learning AI
goal.pos2Before: Help users interested in AI who
goal.pos2Highlight: want to quickly master AI learning
goal.pos3Before: Bring together instructors across fields to share AI tool applications,
goal.pos3Highlight: fostering cross-disciplinary learning and innovative thinking
goal.pos4Before: Through AI tutor, provide users with a
goal.target: Target audience — Students: AI beginners, cross-discipline learners / Instructors: AI experts, educators across fields

keyDecision.label: 05 — KEY DECISION
keyDecision.heading: AI Tutor presentation: tradeoffs of two approaches
keyDecision.intro: The AI tutor is the product's biggest differentiator. When deciding its presentation form, we explored two approaches, each with clear tradeoffs.
keyDecision.optionACons:
Must leave the course page, interrupting learning flow
High page-switching cost
keyDecision.optionBRef: Persistent bottom-right icon → expand chat panel
keyDecision.optionBPros:
Available site-wide, doesn't interrupt current page
Users already have a mature mental model for this pattern
keyDecision.reason: Our AI tutor is positioned as a 'site-wide companion' — not just helping you learn within courses, but also helping you find courses on the homepage and resolving purchase hesitations on course pages. The floating panel covers all User Stories simultaneously. Whether the user is exploring on the homepage, hesitating on a course page, or lost in search results, they can summon the AI tutor at any time.
keyDecision.insightBody:
NN/g research indicates that 'conversation starters' are becoming a standard UI pattern in genAI tools, solving the 'blank canvas problem' — users not knowing what to ask. Our 'context tab' design is based on this insight.

The same research found that users tend to use more direct language with chatbots and heavily rely on preset buttons to reduce input cost.
keyDecision.insightSource: — Nielsen Norman Group, "Prompt Controls in GenAI Chatbots", 2025

deepDive.label: 06 — DESIGN DEEP DIVE
deepDive.heading: Context Tabs — reducing blank canvas cognitive load
deepDive.body:
After opening the chat panel, users face an empty conversation box. According to NN/g research, the core value of use-case prompt suggestions lies in learnability: helping users quickly understand what the AI tool can do.

Based on this insight, we designed three preset context tabs in the chat panel:
deepDive.tab1Desc: Describe your needs in natural language, AI recommends matching courses. More intuitive than traditional filter + keyword search.
deepDive.tab1Example: "I'm a designer, want to learn AI image generation"
deepDive.tab2Desc: While browsing course info, directly ask AI about difficulty, prerequisites, etc., reducing purchase decision uncertainty.
deepDive.tab3Desc: Concept clarification, learning progress suggestions, review highlights — letting AI play a true tutor role.
deepDive.tab3Example: "Summarize the three key points of this chapter"
deepDive.decision: Context tabs balance two goals: reducing first-use cognitive load while preserving an open input field for advanced users to ask freely. This design lets users unfamiliar with AI tools get started immediately, rather than facing a blank input box with no idea what to do.
deepDive.imageCaption: AI Tutor Panel — Preset context tabs + open input

iteration.label: 07 — ITERATION
iteration.heading: Restructuring information hierarchy to amplify product highlights
iteration.body: During the design phase, within our limited time, we further sought guidance and feedback from a mentor. The team rethought the architecture, focused more on the product's key highlights, and iterated on the original homepage design.
iteration.before1: Lacked product character, indistinguishable from competitors
iteration.before2: Course card component details could be improved

finalDesign.body: Designed intuitive exploration and search functionality based on User Stories, enabling users to quickly find courses matching their needs.

finalDesign.video2Caption: Prototype Demo — AI tutor chat panel interaction flow

handoff.heading: UI Flow & Engineering Handoff
handoff.body: Organizing UI Flow based on User Stories and annotating engineering details on the interface is a core part of what I've long been responsible for in past work. So within the limited competition timeline, I rapidly integrated the complete page-transition logic, interaction-state definitions, and component-behavior specs.
handoff.imageCaption: UI Flow — Complete page transition logic & engineering annotations

designSystem.heading: Component State Design & Organization
designSystem.body: (Team Collab) I established the component state specifications and naming logic, while team members completed detailed design for each component.
designSystem.imageCaption: Design System — Component states & interaction specifications

validation.body: This project was completed in August 2023. Our prediction that 'AI tutors will become standard for learning platforms' was fully validated two years later.

reflection.seg1Accent: In this project, my role focused on product style proposals, interface design, and UI Flow with engineering handoff annotations.
reflection.seg1Normal: It was also my first time collaborating with multiple designers on a single project.

Because everyone had different strengths, we could help and learn from each other, while sharpening both my UX thinking and UI expertise. Truly a rewarding experience!

reflection.insight1Body: In just two weeks, the team needed a clear design style anchor to work in parallel. By quickly completing the moodboard and visual proposal early on, four designers could progress independently under a unified design language, significantly reducing late-stage integration conflicts.
reflection.insight2Title: The importance of engineering handoff documents
reflection.insight2Body: UI Flow and engineering annotation deliverables became key to the team's success in this competition — judges evaluated not just beautiful screens, but also the completeness of the handoff.

summary.label: Project Summary
summary.headline: Bringing CEX-level fluidity to on-chain derivatives trading
summary.body: Exora is a perpetual futures trading product built on Hyperliquid. Starting from competitive analysis and user research, I led the visual direction, complete trading flow design, and Mobile PWA experience, and collaborated with front-end engineers to build a dual-layer Token design system supporting multi-tenant brand switching.

context.label: 01 — PROJECT CONTEXT
context.heading: Market Landscape
context.body: CEX and DEX each have clear strengths and weaknesses. This persistent trade-off defines the current state of the crypto derivatives trading market.
context.userProblemCardBody: CEX is smooth but opaque; DEX is transparent but the experience is terrible. This either-or dilemma is a structural problem in the crypto trading market.
context.insightBody: Fluidity and transparency shouldn't be an either-or choice. The real design opportunity is: let users simultaneously get CEX operational efficiency and DEX asset transparency without needing to understand the underlying technology — and the way risk information is presented determines whether this experience is safe or dangerous.

userResearch.label: 03 — TRADING EXPERIENCE BREAKDOWN
userResearch.heading: Deep Analysis of Trading Experience Pain Points
userResearch.body: With 5 years of crypto trading experience, research can reach the core problems faster — not replacing the user perspective, but more precisely identifying which frictions truly affect trading decisions versus surface-level usability issues during research.
userResearch.proseQuote: I clearly wanted to use isolated margin for this position, but after placing the order I realized it was cross-margin 20x.
userResearch.proseContext: This is a real scenario users face when trading on a CEX — when a user switches to a new trading pair, the system defaults to almost cross-margin 20x leverage. Some users are used to controlling risk with isolated margin, yet because of this system default, their entire contract account balance ends up exposed as collateral in a single trade.
userResearch.proseHighlight: The system's default value silently made a high-risk decision for the user,
userResearch.proseContextSuffix: and because the interface design was not prominent, users overlooked important parameter settings before opening a position.
userResearch.proseTakeaway: This experience directly influenced the research focus —
userResearch.proseTakeawayHighlight: locking onto the core journey from "deciding to trade" to "trade completed," identifying critical friction points in the trading flow.
userResearch.trader1Desc: Needs simple onboarding, clear risk information, and foolproof mechanisms.
userResearch.trader2Desc: Extremely sensitive to speed and efficiency. Demands minimal steps, real-time feedback, and uninterrupted flow.
userResearch.trader3Desc: Relies on API stability and ultra-low latency.
userResearch.spectrumFooter:
Onboarding is a one-time barrier, but trading is the daily core experience.
Friction happens here. Retention is lost here.

competitive.label: 02 — COMPETITIVE ANALYSIS
competitive.heading: CEX as UX Baseline, DEX as Direct Competitor
competitive.body: Analyzed 7 exchanges (Binance, OKX, Kraken, Liquid, Hyperliquid, dYdX, Aster) to position Exora's differentiation across three dimensions.
competitive.tableTitle: Breaking the Impossible Triangle: From Trading Venue to Infrastructure Layer
competitive.tableFooter: Exora's opportunity lies in building a SaaS layer: making liquidity and matching engines shared resources, while using design to eliminate DeFi's experience friction.
competitive.insightBody: DEX competitors are all Trading Venues. Exora is a Trading Infrastructure Layer — enabling others to build their own Trading Venue.

designInsight.label: 04 — CORE DESIGN INSIGHT
designInsight.heading: Technical Architecture Is UX's Ceiling — and Its Foundation
designInsight.body: The pre/during/post-trade experience pain points have clear directions for design intervention. But the truly difficult challenge of this project lies one layer deeper — the product architecture involves a six-layer fund entity structure, an Agent Key authorization mechanism, and cross-chain settlement, which are decisions made by the PM and engineering teams. The design challenge is to fully understand the constraints and boundaries of this underlying knowhow, then translate it into a clean user experience.
designInsight.imageCaption: Independently planned the perpetual-contract order flow, interface design, and product visual style

tradingUX.label: 05 — DESIGN OUTPUT: TRADING UX
tradingUX.heading: High-Volatility Position Management: States and Actions Designed for Extreme Decisions
tradingUX.body: Three position states each paired with their own action paths — so users can read risk intensity at a glance and respond immediately when needed.

onboarding.label: 05 — ONBOARDING EXPERIENCE
onboarding.heading: A Role-Based Login Flow
onboarding.body: The front-end replaces cumbersome wallet authorization with a familiar Google login, while the back-end uses a 2FA login flow.

mobilePWA.label: 07 — MOBILE PWA
mobilePWA.heading: Bringing Futures Trading to Mobile
mobilePWA.body: Hyperliquid's mobile is a shrunken copy of desktop. Exora's mobile uses Binance App and OKX App as UX benchmarks, achieving near-native app experience via PWA.
mobilePWA.caption2: Trade — Order Panel fixed bottom · Long-press to prevent mistouch

visualStyle.label: 06 — VISUAL STYLE
visualStyle.heading: A Dark System with Brand Color
visualStyle.body: Through exchange referral systems, airdrops, and new-token mining,
visualStyle.bodyAccent: I've used 10+ exchanges firsthand and continuously track the brand styles and competitive landscape across Web3 projects. A self-maintained watchlist of Web3 products lets me respond and propose quickly during design pitches, while staying sensitive to emerging design trends.

designSystem.label: 07 — DESIGN SYSTEM
designSystem.heading: Building a Scalable Design Language
designSystem.body: Led the product style, building and maintaining a complete Design System with one-click Light / Dark Mode switching, making it easier for designers on the team to collaborate.

collaboration.label: 08 — AI TOOLING FOR DESIGN SYSTEMS
collaboration.heading: AI-Driven Design Applications
collaboration.body: Built a multi-tenant, multi-theme Design System tool with front-end collaboration using Claude Code, anticipating that the core product will need to ship multi-tenant design system variants in the future.

impact.heading: How Design Influenced Product Outcomes

reflection.label: 11 — REFLECTION
reflection.heading: Reflections on Designing in High-Volatility Markets

card1.title: Finding the right problem through a trader's lens
card1.body: 5 years of crypto trading experience let research go straight to "the frictions that actually affect order decisions," instead of stopping at "the interface is hard to use." Research focused on the core journey from <highlight>"deciding to trade" to "trade completed"</highlight> — rather than generic UX improvements.

card2.title: Subtraction is harder than addition
card2.body: A perp trader has to watch price, position, funding rate, liquidation price, margin ratio — adding more is easy; the challenge is <highlight>showing only what the user needs at each decision point</highlight>. From there, it's about deciding which information should be pushed to a second layer, and which earns a spot on the main canvas.

card3.title: Friction isn't always worth removing
card3.body: In crypto finance, <highlight>"reducing risk" and "reducing friction" often point in opposite directions</highlight> — making a flow too smooth can lead users to place orders before fully reading the risk. The work isn't to strip out as many steps as possible; it's to judge which frictions should stay as protective mechanisms.

tradingJourney.preRow1Pain: The silent default of leverage and margin mode
tradingJourney.preRow1Desc: When switching to a new trading pair, the system defaults to cross-margin 20x leverage — with no prominent design and no reminder.
tradingJourney.preRow1Opportunity: Present the margin-mode default in a distinct UI style, so users clearly know “this value is the single most critical factor when placing an order.”
tradingJourney.preRow2Pain: No liquidation price visible before placing an order
tradingJourney.preRow2Desc: The liquidation price only appears after a position is opened. At the moment of ordering, you don’t know “at what price this trade gets liquidated,” and have to open a calculator and enter it manually.
tradingJourney.preRow2Opportunity: Calculate and show the estimated liquidation price in real time in the order panel, so the risk boundary is visible before ordering.
tradingJourney.duringRow1Pain: DEX orders require repeated wallet confirmations
tradingJourney.duringRow1Desc: Traditional DEX: tap order → wallet popup → manual confirm → wait for broadcast → fill. Every trade interrupts the flow of thought — hugely costly in fast-moving markets.
tradingJourney.duringRow1Opportunity: The Agent Key mechanism turns ordering into: tap → instant fill, reducing the technical operation back to a pure trading decision.
tradingJourney.duringRow2Pain: Accumulated funding-rate cost is not obvious
tradingJourney.duringRow2Desc: The position panel doesn’t show “how much funding rate this position has been charged so far.” A user who thinks they’re up 2% may, after deductions, be left with only 1.3% — or even a loss.
tradingJourney.duringRow2Opportunity: Show accumulated funding rate at the position level, improving data readability and transparency.
tradingJourney.postRow1Desc: The position panel consolidates all risk-control information — grasp the full position in a single screen.
tradingJourney.postRow1Opportunity: The position panel consolidates all key risk-control information — grasp the full position in a single screen.

hero.label: WEB3 · VIDEO PLATFORM
hero.title: A Web3 All-in-One Video Platform for Crypto Creators & Viewers
hero.subtitle: Hong Kong Cyberport Programme Finalist

meta.scopeValue: UI UX Design, Feature Planning, Logo Design, Pitch Deck Design

context.label: 01 — PROJECT CONTEXT
context.heading: Building a Video Platform Where Projects, KOLs & Web3 Users All Thrive
context.body:
The founding team were crypto content creators who experienced two core pain points firsthand — mainstream video platforms impose policy restrictions on Web3 content (throttling, banned promo links, takedown risks), directly impacting creator reach and revenue. Meanwhile, Web3 information is scattered across Twitter, Telegram, YouTube, and more, with inconsistent quality and no trusted aggregation hub.

After identifying these market pain points, they decided to build a Web3 all-in-one video platform, starting with the Chinese-speaking market.
context.img1Caption: Requirements workshop with the founding team

problemDefinition.label: 02 — COMPETITIVE POSITIONING
problemDefinition.heading: Competitive Analysis & Platform Positioning
problemDefinition.body: Analyzing competitors from the perspective of each user role to identify competitive advantages and define platform positioning.
problemDefinition.group1Card1Adv1: More professional, comprehensive Web3 video content aggregation
problemDefinition.group1Card1Adv2: Systematic categorization aligned with market trends
problemDefinition.calloutBody: Build a video platform where all three roles (creators, viewers, projects) gain value, differentiated through Web3-native mechanics (wallet tasks, points, airdrops).

marketResearch.label: 04 — MARKET RESEARCH
marketResearch.heading: Global Crypto Users Growing Rapidly — Chinese Market Scale Supports MVP
marketResearch.body: According to Crypto.com and Triple-A market reports, Chinese-speaking crypto users reached approximately 60 million by 2023. With favorable policies and Bitcoin halving/ETF narratives, crypto user growth in 2024 is expected to be explosive.
marketResearch.calloutCard1Body: Massive new user influx means onboarding must be beginner-friendly — cannot assume wallet literacy.
marketResearch.calloutCard2Body: Chinese market scale is sufficient to support a Chinese-first MVP strategy.
marketResearch.calloutCard3Body: Rapid market cycles mean content categorization and update speed are core experience, not add-on features.

marketOpportunity.label: 05 — MARKET OPPORTUNITY
marketOpportunity.heading: The Potential Value of Web3 Information & Video Platforms
marketOpportunity.body: From interviews with Web3 media professionals, I learned that market trends and hotspots update extremely fast — information distribution must be "fast, precise, and impactful." In this context, Web3 information distribution compensation shows exceptional cost-effectiveness, making Web3 video platforms a highly promising opportunity.

platformDecision.label: 06 — PLATFORM DECISION
platformDecision.heading: Balancing Development Resources & User Experience
platformDecision.body: Web3 is a fast-paced industry with tight development timelines. With limited resources, I evaluated three development directions across development cost, user experience, and wallet integration complexity.
platformDecision.optionAPros:
Low development cost, ideal for rapid MVP validation
Cross-platform, no App Store review restrictions
Users prefer connecting wallets on desktop — smoothest Web integration experience
platformDecision.optionBCons:
Long development cycle
Web3 content may be removed by App Store / Google Play
Wallet integration requires WalletConnect — added complexity
platformDecision.optionCCons:
High wallet integration complexity
Offline scenarios irrelevant for video platforms
Service Worker maintenance cost
platformDecision.reason: We chose Web-first. Beyond resource considerations, the core reason is that most users — due to security awareness — still prefer desktop for on-chain interactions (wallet connections, transaction signing). Web provides the smoothest wallet integration experience.

competitiveAnalysis.label: 07 — COMPETITIVE ANALYSIS
competitiveAnalysis.heading: Analyzing Web3 Competitors to Extract Design Insights
competitiveAnalysis.body: Analyzed five Web3 video platform competitors — Odysee, 3Speak, DLive, D.Tube, and REVO — focusing on three core dimensions to identify product entry opportunities for Web3Vid.
competitiveAnalysis.card1Body: Odysee supports uploading any file format (video, music, ebooks); 3Speak lets creators build their own token markets. But users ultimately care about "is there good content," not decentralized storage itself.
competitiveAnalysis.card1Highlight: decentralization as infrastructure, not selling point
competitiveAnalysis.card2Body: All five competitors bind their own tokens (LBC, Hive/Speak, Lemons, DTUB, R3VO), but tokens lack liquidity with few early users. DLive takes 25% commission; D.Tube uploads consume VP voting power — barriers too high.
competitiveAnalysis.card2Highlight: Start with points system to validate mechanics
competitiveAnalysis.card3Body: D.Tube uses IPFS with public data but no algorithmic recommendations; REVO combines video with NFTs but is overly complex. Web3 video platforms generally have rough UX and high onboarding barriers.

designPrinciples.label: 08 — DESIGN PRINCIPLES
designPrinciples.heading: Three Core Principles from Research to Design
designPrinciples.body: Synthesizing early research, I established three design principles to guide all subsequent UI/UX decisions. Each principle directly responds to problems discovered during the research phase.
designPrinciples.card1Body: Users' mental model for watching videos doesn't need to be relearned (aligned with YouTube). Web3 features (wallet connection, points, airdrops) are layered on as enhancements. Reduce cognitive barriers, increase Web3 feature adoption.
designPrinciples.card2Body: Every feature must answer: "What value does this bring to creators, viewers, and projects respectively?" If it only serves one role, lower its priority. Ensure positive ecosystem circulation.
designPrinciples.card3Body: Use points in the MVP phase to validate user behavior models, avoiding premature token economics that bring compliance and liquidity risks. Data first, reduce decision risk.
designPrinciples.ownershipTag: I led — The three principles were proposed by me after competitive analysis and interviews, then confirmed by team discussion.

productPositioning.label: 03 — PRODUCT POSITIONING
productPositioning.heading: Defining the Business Model & Product Value
productPositioning.body: Positioned the product as a Web3 Chinese-language video platform, serving as a blockchain media hub for the Chinese-speaking market, providing curated, real-time, comprehensive industry information.
productPositioning.calloutBody: After analyzing competitors from each user type's perspective, I converged on three key differentiators: ① Zero content censorship for Web3, creator revenue unaffected by platform policies. ② Native interaction via wallet tasks, viewer engagement depth far exceeding traditional platforms. ③ Precision ad channel reaching active crypto users, higher project ad efficiency.
productPositioning.img1Caption: Competitive advantage comparison by user type

designDecision.label: 09 — DESIGN DECISION
designDecision.heading: How to Keep Users Coming Back to Web3Vid?
designDecision.body: Retention mechanisms are critical to platform survival. I evaluated three approaches across short-term DAU lift, long-term ecosystem health, and MVP feasibility, ultimately choosing a points-based task system as the primary strategy.
designDecision.optionACons:
Insufficient content during cold start, retention inevitably low
Cannot validate quickly in MVP stage
designDecision.optionAVerdict: Rejected — Long-term direction, but not MVP priority
designDecision.optionBPros:
Effectively boosts short-term DAU
Instant positive feedback, maintains activity during cold start
Points data serves as behavioral baseline for future token economics
designDecision.optionBCons: May attract reward farmers (anti-cheat mechanisms needed)
designDecision.optionCCons:
MVP user base too small, social features will feel empty
High dev cost, distracts from core experience
designDecision.optionCVerdict: Rejected — User Base Insufficient to Support
designDecision.calloutBody: B (points task system) as primary, A as long-term direction. The MVP priority is quickly validating whether users will watch videos on this platform. Points provide instant positive feedback, maintaining user activity even when content volume isn't rich enough. Meanwhile, points data serves as a behavioral baseline for future token economics.
designDecision.ownershipTag: I led — The three-option comparison and final decision were proposed and led by me in team discussions.

behavioralDesign.label: 10 — BEHAVIORAL DESIGN
behavioralDesign.heading: Behavioral Psychology-Driven Points Mechanism Design
behavioralDesign.body: After confirming the points task system, I applied behavioral psychology principles to design specific reward mechanisms — ensuring it's not just "having points" but making the points system genuinely change user behavior.
behavioralDesign.card1Before: Based on B.F. Skinner's operant conditioning theory — when behavior is rewarded, users are more likely to repeat it. After completing a task,
behavioralDesign.card1After: to reinforce the "behavior → reward" psychological connection.
behavioralDesign.card2Before: Applying the Goal Gradient Effect — the closer to the goal, the stronger the motivation. Designed a
behavioralDesign.card2After: so users can see how many points remain until the reward — the "almost there" feeling drives the last mile.
behavioralDesign.card3After: keep users returning because they "don't want to break their streak."

featureDesign.label: 11 — FEATURE DESIGN
featureDesign.heading: Merging Web2 & Web3 for a New Feature Experience
featureDesign.body: Combining familiar video watching interfaces with Web3 wallet task functionality. Core design strategy: make Web2 parts "require no learning" while Web3 parts are "worth exploring."
featureDesign.story1After: , I can connect my wallet while watching videos, complete on-chain tasks to earn points, giving my viewing behavior direct returns.
featureDesign.story2After: , I can bind interactive tasks to my videos, deepening viewer engagement while earning project collaboration revenue.
featureDesign.story3After: , I can distribute native ads via wallet tasks, precisely reaching active crypto users who have connected their wallets.

coreFlow.label: 12 — CORE FLOW
coreFlow.heading: Wallet Tasks × Points Lottery: The Platform Core Flow
coreFlow.body: The video platform combined with wallet task lottery flow is Web3Vid's core differentiator. I designed a "Watch → Connect → Complete → Reward" closed-loop flow, letting users naturally encounter Web3 interactions during their viewing experience.
coreFlow.ownershipTag: I led — This core flow was independently designed by me, from User Flow to UI details.
coreFlow.flowCaption: Complete Wallet Task → Points → Lottery User Flow
coreFlow.img1Caption: Wallet connection flow — supports MetaMask, WalletConnect

informationArchitecture.label: 13 — INFORMATION ARCHITECTURE
informationArchitecture.heading: Designing a Web3 Category System — Balancing Browsing & Search
informationArchitecture.body: Web3 has numerous tracks. I designed a dual-layer categorization architecture so users with different goals can quickly find the content they want.
informationArchitecture.text:
Main Categories (Tab level): Trending, Breaking News, Market Analysis, Hot Topics, Tutorials, Airdrop Guides, Deep Dives — helping users immediately find their area of interest.

Sub-categories (Hashtag level): Video hashtags provide more precise topic filtering (e.g., #BTCHalving #Layer2 #DeFi), suitable for users with clear goals.

Category items were determined through Web3 KOL content topic frequency analysis and team industry experience, identifying the top 7 high-frequency themes as main categories.

uiDesign.label: 14 — UI DESIGN
uiDesign.heading: Integrating Research into an MVP That Fits Product Positioning
uiDesign.body: Platform video content includes long-form videos, short videos, and podcast audio. Considering existing user habits, the main viewing flow mirrors YouTube. Core differentiation lies in wallet interactions, points tasks, and Web3-styled lottery design.
uiDesign.img2Caption: Player — Video viewing & wallet task entry

designSystem.label: 15 — DESIGN SYSTEM
designSystem.heading: Building a Design System for Consistency & Development Efficiency
designSystem.body: To ensure rapid MVP iteration doesn't sacrifice visual consistency, I established a Design System early in the design process, covering colors, typography, and component specifications.
designSystem.ownershipTag: I led — Design System was independently built and maintained by me.

pitchDeck.label: 16 — PITCH DECK
pitchDeck.heading: Pitch Deck Design
pitchDeck.body: I was responsible for integrating product positioning, market analysis, and competitive advantages into an investor pitch deck, used for the Hong Kong Cyberport Incubation Programme application — ultimately reaching the finals.

scalability.label: 17 — SCALABILITY
scalability.heading: Scale Challenges & Mitigation Strategies Anticipated During Design
scalability.body: MVP design can't only look at the present. During the design process, I anticipated scale challenges that would emerge as the product grows, and reserved architectural expansion space.
scalability.card1Body: The existing 7 main categories won't suffice, and hashtags will explode. The architecture reserves positions for "custom categories" and "hashtag search," with algorithmic recommendations planned long-term.
scalability.card2Title: Expanding from Chinese to English Markets
scalability.card2Body: UI copy, category names, and content recommendation logic all need i18n. Design System text components use auto-layout, reserving space for multilingual support.
scalability.card3Body: Many users will only farm points without actually watching videos. Points task design includes a "watch duration threshold" (at least 70% completion), rather than counting mere opens.

hero.label: WEB3 ・ FINTECH ・ DASHBOARD
hero.title: A Stable Annualized Compounding Bot Platform
hero.subtitle: Packaging Bitfinex's automated lending algorithm into a product everyday investors can actually use

meta.resultValue: Pilot users saw ~50% higher average APR; exhibited at the 2023 Taoyuan Youth Entrepreneurship Expo; pitched to NCU Angel Ventures
meta.scopeValue: Competitive analysis, feature planning, UX / UI design, design system, logo design, pitch-deck design, expo poster design

background.label: 01 — BACKGROUND
background.heading: The Bitfinex lending market: high returns, but a steep experience barrier
background.intro: Bitfinex is one of the oldest crypto exchanges in the world. Its P2P lending market lets users lend idle USD or stablecoins to margin traders and earn interest. In recent years the average annual percentage rate (APR) has run around 10–20%, far above traditional bank foreign-currency deposits (about 1.1% in Taiwan, about 4% in the US).
background.challengeTitle: Manual lending has too high an operational barrier
background.challengeBody: Users have to continuously monitor market rates, manually adjust order parameters, and absorb the efficiency loss of idle capital.
background.solutionTitle: Using the Bitfinex API to optimize lending efficiency
background.solutionBody: An engineer on the team built a higher-performance lending algorithm that automates the lending decisions that previously had to be made by hand.
background.taskTitle: Package the algorithm into a product everyday investors can use
background.taskBody: Turn this algorithm into a clear, trustworthy, low-barrier product experience — Rolling.

whyNow.title: Why Now — why this moment?
whyNow.intro: Rolling's development timing was tightly tied to the crypto market cycle:
whyNow.bullet1: A bull market was projected to arrive between Q2 2024, sharply increasing the number of people buying and holding BTC
whyNow.bullet2: Lending APR around a bull run is usually significantly higher than usual — the best window to acquire users for a lending product
whyNow.bullet3: Bull–bear transition points bring a flood of new investors — exactly the core audience who "want to earn interest but don't want high volatility"
whyNow.conclusion: From a long-term investment lens, the market cycle gives a low-risk, stable-yield product like Rolling a natural demand tailwind.

competitive.label: 02 — COMPETITIVE ANALYSIS
competitive.heading: Breaking down 5 experience problems in the market leader, Fuly.ai
competitive.body: Before designing Rolling, I analyzed the competitors in the lending market and identified four main rivals:

table.row1Feature: IBRR algorithm, smart copy-trading mode, AI risk indicators
table.row1Weakness: Tedious onboarding, non-real-time bot status, unintuitive earnings reports
table.row2Weakness: Complex dual-fee structure, dated interface, polarized reviews on returns
table.row3Weakness: Confusing tiered pricing, high barrier on premium plans, short 14-day trial
table.row4Feature: Real-time order updates, auto-refresh every 5 minutes, BTC DCA support
table.row4Weakness: Only 3 currencies, low brand awareness, insufficient community trust

competitive.caption: Rolling's differentiated positioning: an edge on both “beginner-friendliness” and “stable yield”
competitive.fulyIntro: Fuly.ai is the most direct competitor (also a Bitfinex lending bot), so I did a deeper UX teardown of it:

pain1.title: Onboarding takes 6 steps — a very high barrier for newcomers
pain1.body: To get set up on Fuly.ai, a user has to: register a Fuly account → register a Bitfinex account → complete KYC verification → generate an API key on Bitfinex (turning on exactly 5 permissions) → paste the API key back into Fuly → move funds from the exchange wallet to the funding wallet. If any step goes wrong, the bot won’t run.
pain1.note: Note: Bitfinex's KYC review is fairly strict, and identity verification can take several business days.

pain2.title: Bot startup is delayed and status feedback is lacking
pain2.body: After funds are deposited, Fuly.ai's bot takes a while before it starts placing orders, and the order information isn't updated in real time. Users can't confirm “is the bot actually working?” — for a financial product involving real money, that's a serious trust problem.

pain3.title: Performance reports lack intuitiveness
pain3.body: Fuly.ai's reports are relatively basic and rarely show clearly how a user can quickly grasp their earnings trend on the dashboard.

competitive.auditTitle: Three key frictions that block newcomers
competitive.auditIntro: From sign-up to activation to viewing reports, breaking down the points where users are most likely to drop off, step by step.
competitive.auditFocusBody: Sign-up flow complexity, system-status feedback, performance-information clarity
competitive.auditImageAlt: Three key frictions that block newcomers
competitive.auditCaption: Fuly.ai's dashboard has an unclear visual hierarchy, and its performance reports lack intuitiveness

strategy.label: 03 — DESIGN STRATEGY
strategy.heading: From "6 steps, 30 minutes" to "2 steps, 5 minutes"
strategy.body: Based on the findings from the competitive analysis, I defined Rolling’s core design strategy as: <highlight>use a corporate-account architecture to lower the entry barrier, and use dashboard design to build ongoing trust.</highlight>

table.row1Rolling: A corporate account manages everything: customers don’t need to do their own KYC or generate an API — users just “register → choose a plan → deposit → start earning”
table.row2Rolling: The dashboard home shows three core metrics in real time (cumulative ROI, today’s P&L, cumulative interest), with daily-updated earnings details
table.row3Rolling: The earnings overview consolidates currency, date, ROI, and amount, with trend charts planned for the future

before.tag: Fuly.ai — about 30 minutes to several days

targetUser.label: 04 — TARGET USERS & USER STORY
targetUser.heading: Targeting three user types, converging core needs from competitor pain points

ta1.title: Crypto-market beginners
ta1.body: People interested in crypto but scared off by complex operating interfaces. What they need is a “just put it in and earn” experience, not a pile of parameter settings. This is also the user group <highlight>Fuly.ai and Bitfinex’s native tools lose the most.</highlight>

ta2.title: Steady, low-risk investors
ta2.body: People with investment experience who don't want to bear crypto price volatility. Lending's “lend out capital, collect interest” model naturally fits their risk appetite.

ta3.title: Long-term investors
ta3.body: People who believe in compounding and are willing to hold long term and let their capital keep rolling. Rolling's product naming and auto-compounding mechanism were designed for exactly this group.

targetUser.story1: As an investor, I want to “see my investment performance at a glance,” so I can understand my gains and losses without opening a spreadsheet to calculate.
targetUser.story2: As an investor, I want to “review daily investment details,” so I can confirm the automated trading bot is genuinely working.
targetUser.story3: As an investor, I want to “withdraw funds anytime,” so I can rest assured my assets won’t be locked up — lowering the psychological barrier to trying a new platform.
targetUser.storyHeading: Converging core needs from user scenarios
targetUser.storyIntro: Translating competitor pain points into three questions the product must answer directly.

featurePlanning.label: 05 — FEATURE PLANNING
featurePlanning.heading: Planning the overall product features through user scenarios
featurePlanning.body: Based on the three user stories and the experience gaps identified in the competitive analysis, I drafted Rolling’s feature architecture and information fields. The core principle: every page should directly answer the one question the user cares about most.
featurePlanning.sitemapHeading: Converged into six core feature modules
featurePlanning.sitemapBody: I converged the user scenarios into a fitting set of feature categories: asset overview, wallet (deposit / withdraw / records), interest earnings, notifications, account management, and API permission settings — plus proof of reserves as a supporting trust entry point. Each module maps to a clear user task.

decisions.label: 06 — DESIGN DECISIONS
decisions.heading: The design decisions that shaped the product experience
decisions.body: Below are three key decisions I made while designing the Rolling dashboard. Each went through multiple options and trade-offs.

d1.title: Asset overview: what should users see first?
d1.question: A lending platform has a lot of data — total assets, live rates, cumulative interest, daily rate, ROI, today's P&L. The information density of the dashboard's first screen directly determines users' sense of trust and retention.

optionA.title: Option A: one big number
optionA.desc: Show only total assets; tuck everything else below
optionA.cons: Users have to scroll to see performance

optionB.title: Option B: three cards side by side
optionB.desc: Cumulative ROI, today's P&L, and cumulative interest side by side
optionB.pros: Answers the three core questions at a glance

optionC.title: Option C: gauge-style
optionC.cons: Visually striking but takes a lot of space

callout.title: Final decision: Option B — three cards side by side
callout.body: Every time a lending user logs in, they most want three questions answered: “How is my return?” “How much did I earn today?” “How much cumulative interest?” The three cards map to these three core questions.

d2.title: Decision ② Earnings presentation: table vs. chart?
d2.question: Should earnings detail use a “table with precise numbers” or a “line chart where the trend is obvious at a glance”? Each has advantages, depending on the user’s scenario.

callout.title: Final decision: ship Option A in v1, plan Option C for v2
callout.body: Given limited development resources at the MVP stage, I first used a table to satisfy the core “auditing” need. But I simultaneously produced a v2 concept (chart + table combo) to iterate on once user volume reaches a certain scale.

d3.title: Decision ③ Trust design: how do you make users comfortable handing money to a bot?
d3.question: The user’s biggest psychological hurdle isn’t “is the rate high enough” but “is it safe?” The team had already built a Bitfinex reserve-tracking mechanism (continuously monitoring the exchange’s wallet addresses and token allocation), but none of that security information was reflected on the dashboard.

optionA.title: Option A: passive
optionA.desc: Explain the security mechanism on an FAQ page
optionA.cons: Lowest cost but least effective — users won't go look for it

optionB.title: Option B: embedded
optionB.desc: Add a “platform health” status card to the dashboard
optionB.pros: Shows Bitfinex reserve amount and token allocation in real time

optionC.title: Option C: notification
optionC.desc: Only push an alert when something is abnormal
optionC.cons: Saves space but can't build trust day to day

callout.title: Final decision: Option B — embed Proof of Reserves status in the dashboard
callout.body: Trust shouldn’t be passive. Especially for users new to crypto finance, seeing real-time figures right on the dashboard home — “Bitfinex reserves $5.2B, BTC 59%, ETH 9.7%” — effectively lowers trust anxiety. This design turned the security argument the team had only put in the pitch deck into a UI element users see every day.

designSystem.label: 08 — DESIGN SYSTEM
designSystem.heading: A visual system built for the lending scenario
designSystem.body: Rolling's design system is built on a dark theme paired with high-contrast functional colors. <highlight>The dark theme was chosen for two reasons: the professional tone common to financial products, and the visual comfort for lending users who may check their assets in the evening.</highlight>

branding.label: 09 — BRANDING
branding.heading: Stable compounding, like a rolling snowball
branding.body:
Because the product’s core is a low-risk, long-term, stable-compounding automated lending bot whose gains grow larger over time, I named it Rolling. The logo wraps a dynamic “R” inside a hexagon (echoing crypto’s geometric language), conveying continuous rolling and growth.

The brand visuals extended to the pitch deck (used for the NCU Angel Ventures pitch) and the expo poster (used at the 2023 Taoyuan Youth Entrepreneurship Expo), ensuring consistency in outward communication.

results.label: 10 — OUTCOME
results.heading: ~50% APR improvement in the pilot phase
results.body1: In the pilot phase, I tested with 10 users; the Rolling bot's average APR was about 15–20%, roughly a 50% improvement over the 10–13% of manual lending. The gains came mainly from three areas: the bot periodically auto-refreshing orders to reduce idle-capital time, reacting within minutes when rates briefly spiked (e.g., the market hitting 30% APR in April 2024), and auto-compounding contributions accumulating long-term benefit.
results.body2: On the business side, the team targeted a lending pool of 120,000 USDT; modeling 10% APR with compounding projected a yield pool of about 99,200 USDT — figures that were also central to the business-model feasibility argument in the angel-ventures pitch.
results.disclaimer: Note: returns are based on public Bitfinex USD lending-market data and industry benchmarks; actual returns fluctuate with market supply and demand.
results.qualitative1: Pitched at NCU Angel Ventures, completing the product proposal and business-model presentation
results.qualitative2: Exhibited at the 2023 Taoyuan Youth Entrepreneurship Expo, demonstrating the product to investors and potential users
results.qualitative3: Independently delivered the full brand visual suite (logo, dashboard UI, pitch deck, expo poster, design system)

card1.title: What went well
card1.body: Starting from competitors’ UX problems to define the design strategy gave every design decision a clear “why.” Using a corporate-account architecture to dramatically simplify the user’s entry barrier was this product’s most core differentiating design.

card2.title: What could be better
card2.body: If I did it again, I’d run more complete user testing early in the design — at least 3–5 target users doing task-based testing — to validate design assumptions with data rather than guesswork.

card3.title: What I took away
card3.body: When designing in crypto finance, <highlight>“trust” carries far more weight than “good looks.”</highlight> Whether users are willing to put in real money depends on whether the product can answer “is it safe?” at every touchpoint. This insight shaped how I thought about features in my later Web3-related projects.

hero.label: WEB3 ・ TELEGRAM GAME ・ PLAY TO EARN
hero.title: Play to Earn GameFi
hero.subtitle: Starting from an 8-page whitepaper, I built the visual language, UX flow, and player-onboarding narrative for a Web3 Telegram mini-game in 2.5 weeks.

meta.scopeValue: UI/UX design, IP illustration, feature-planning lead, logo design, deck design

background.label: 01 — BACKGROUND
background.heading: Amid the Tap-to-Earn craze, building a mini-game's design language from scratch
background.body: In mid-2024, Hamster Combat surpassed 100 million monthly active players, and Tap-to-Earn became the hottest entry model in the Telegram ecosystem. The project team seized this market window, planning to finish the visuals and UX within weeks of completing the whitepaper and then launch a public sale.
background.constraintTitle: The only design reference was an 8-page whitepaper document
background.constraintBody: The document covered the game mechanics, token economy (G8 Coin), and technical architecture (AWS + Next.js + BSC smart contracts), but lacked any comprehensive planning of the product’s features and flows. Every design decision had to be derived from the whitepaper myself.

coreProblem.label: 02 — CORE DESIGN PROBLEM
coreProblem.heading: How do you get a new Web3 player through the full game loop?
coreProblem.question: How do you build a visual language and UX flow so that even a player who has never touched Web3 can smoothly complete the full game loop of “deposit → buy a chick → tap to interact → claim rewards”?
coreProblem.card1Body: The IP character, brand colors, and component language all had to be built from scratch — and quickly form a commercially viable game look.
coreProblem.card2Body: Web3 actions like USDT deposits and on-chain interactions on BSC had to be packaged into a flow new players could understand.
coreProblem.card3Body: The token-reward mechanism couldn’t just convey wins and losses — it also had to manage players’ expectations around reward uncertainty.

insight.label: 03 — DESIGN INSIGHT FROM THE PLAYER’S VIEW
insight.heading: Combining my own everyday Web3 experience to organize the feature plan effectively
insight.body: Drawing on my past experience playing Hamster Combat, I combined a former player’s perspective with design thinking. Based on the whitepaper, I quickly mapped out a UX flow better suited to the project team’s needs.

aiTools.label: 04 — AI TOOLS ACCELERATING EARLY PROPOSALS

visualSystem.label: 05 — VISUAL SYSTEM
visualSystem.heading: Consistency from IP to components
visualSystem.body: After establishing the IP style, I systematically extended the illustration’s visual language to the UI components, so players feel the same brand world across the logo, the IP character, and every interface touchpoint.
visualSystem.imgAlt: IP visual language extended to UI components
visualSystem.principle1Body: Create a cartoon feel and sense of boundary, reinforcing the tappability of clickable objects.

hero.label: Case Study — 2023
hero.title:
35 Social Platform
Online-Merge-Offline
Dating for Grown-ups
hero.subtitle: An OMO social platform designed for second chances, late marriage, and single parents — letting online connections extend into real, offline interaction within a safe, friendly environment.

summary.label: PROJECT SUMMARY
summary.heading: Taiwan’s first OMO social platform built specifically for the 35+ demographic.
summary.body: 35 Social Platform is Taiwan’s first OMO social platform designed for people aged 35 and over. As the sole designer, I led the product design from 0 to 1 — from client requirement interviews, competitive analysis, and information architecture to the complete PWA dating platform and brand website. The design output served directly as the core visual material for the Ministry of Economic Affairs’ SBIR grant application, <highlight>helping the client successfully secure government funding</highlight>.

problem.heading: A 3.93-million-person need, ignored by the entire market
problem.body: Taiwan is simultaneously experiencing aging, later marriage, and a high divorce rate. Over a decade, the mature single population aged 35–64 grew by more than 1 million, while the marriage-age single population aged 25–34 shrank by 140,000 — the center of gravity of the dating market is shifting, but product design hasn’t kept up.
problem.calloutHeading: 1.75 million mature singles with prior marriage experience, with no product built for them
problem.calloutBody: Mature singles make up 17% of the national population, and 45% of them are divorced or widowed — these 1.75 million people have prior marriage experience, more mature expectations for relationships, and more complex real-life considerations (children, finances, rebuilding social circles). They aren’t “edge-case dating-app users”; they are a complete, overlooked market.
problem.imageLabel: Taiwan single-population trend — the crossover of rising mature singles vs. declining marriage-age singles
problem.gapTitle: It’s not a lack of features — the product assumptions were never built for these people
problem.gapBody: Existing dating platforms are uniformly designed around 18–30-year-old users — lightweight, fast, looks-driven. This design logic has a structural gap with what the 35+ group needs: “a sense of safety, deep understanding, real offline interaction.” This isn’t a problem of missing features — it’s that <highlight>the entire product assumption was never built for these people</highlight>.

competitive.heading: The market gap: 30+ × serious relationships
competitive.body: After plotting Taiwan’s major dating platforms on a quadrant of “age positioning” and “relationship seriousness,” the top-right corner (30+ × serious relationships) is almost empty — only Qianshou 50 (766K members) reaches this segment, but its product form leans toward traditional matchmaking services and lacks the experience of a modern social platform.
competitive.imageLabel: Competitive positioning map — age × relationship-seriousness quadrant, marking Tinder / Paktor / Qianshou 50, etc.
competitive.insightTitle: Social scenarios matter more than the matching algorithm
competitive.insightBody: The market gap isn’t just age coverage — it’s a gap in product form. What the 35+ group needs isn’t “Tinder but a bit older,” but a social platform that fully connects online to offline (OMO) — single-parent family trips, mature-age light travel, talks and meetups, relationship advisors. <highlight>Social scenarios matter more than the matching algorithm</highlight>.

process.heading: 0 → 1: from requirement interviews to design delivery
process.body: As the sole designer, I started from scratch — discussing feature requirements with the client, organizing the overall feature plan, and finally producing and handing off the design to engineers. The whole process had four phases, with design, engineering, and client-side tasks advancing in parallel.
process.step1Body: I held several rounds of requirement interviews with the founder to define the MVP feature scope, inventory existing resources and technical constraints, and compile a complete requirements list. The client had 15 years of e-commerce experience and a clear market read on the product; the designer’s role was to translate that business vision into an executable product structure.
process.step2Body: Three sides advanced in sync: design ran competitive analysis, feature planning, and wireframing; engineering researched the Ministry of the Interior identity-verification API and payment-integration options; the client set membership pricing rules and prepared legal documents like terms of use and privacy policy.
process.step3Body: I created multi-direction visual proposals on key screens, so the client could make a style decision on concrete screens rather than abstract descriptions.
process.step4Body: Once the style was locked, I expanded into full-page design — meeting regularly with the client and engineers to dynamically adjust the design based on technical feasibility and business needs.

style.heading: Finding a visual language that’s “warm but not childish”
style.body: The 35+ group’s visual preferences differ sharply from younger users — too flashy reads as not serious enough, too corporate loses social warmth. The proposal phase explored multiple style directions and finally converged on a “warm, mature, trustworthy” visual tone, so the platform signals a different positioning from Tinder and Bumble at first glance.
style.imageLabel: Design style proposals — the exploration of multiple directions

pwa.heading: A mobile-first dating experience
pwa.body: Built as a PWA so users can use it without downloading from the App Store. Core features cover profile creation, match browsing, chat, and event sign-up — integrating the full journey from meeting online to meeting offline within a single product.

web.heading: Brand image and content entry point
web.body: Beyond the PWA dating platform, I designed the brand website and blog system in parallel. The brand pages convey positioning and trust to the outside world, while the blog serves as an SEO content entry point and an extension of community building — continuously bringing organic traffic to the platform.

impact.heading: How design shaped the product outcomes
impact.body: From winning the grant to launching and operating the product, the design output had concrete impact on multiple levels.
impact.metric1Label: Successfully won the MOEA SBIR grant
impact.metric2Label: Surpassed 10,000 members within 10 months of launch
impact.metric3Label: PWA + web designed end-to-end by one person

impact.card1Body: The designs served directly as the core visual material for the MOEA SBIR grant application, concretely presenting the product positioning, user flow, and platform style, and helping the review committee understand the product’s market differentiation and feasibility. Design quality directly affected the proposal’s persuasiveness.

impact.card2Body: The platform entered official trial operation in February 2024 and surpassed 10,000 members by December 2024. During this period the client continued partnering with the Taoyuan City Government Youth Affairs Bureau on public-interest events, taking the product from design concept to real social impact.

testimonial.quote: “The final deliverables not only met expectations — they exceeded them.”
testimonial.body: Truly grateful for JS’s professionalism and attention to detail, ensuring every design detail was thoroughly considered so the design is <highlight>both practical and beautiful</highlight>. Throughout communication, JS always listened patiently to needs and grasped the direction precisely. Working with JS was a pleasure — a truly reliable partner!

reflection.heading: Understanding the client’s problem matters more than understanding their requirements
reflection.p1: This was a 1.5-month, one-person 0-to-1 client project. Looking back, the most critical design decision didn’t happen in Figma — it happened during the requirement-interview phase.
reflection.p2: The client came with a clear market read: she knew the 35+ mature single demographic was an overlooked market, and she knew OMO was the right product form. <highlight>The designer’s value wasn’t to tell her “what to build,” but to translate her business intuition into a product structure users could understand.</highlight>
reflection.p3: After launch, membership quickly broke 10,000 — validating one thing: when a market gap is real enough, design’s job isn’t to create demand, but to <highlight>remove friction — so the right people can find the platform built for them with the lowest possible barrier</highlight>.

hero.title: A course-booking platform: bilateral system design from a 2C booking app to a 2B merchant backend
hero.subtitle: Turning the client’s vague brief of “build a Taiwanese ClassPass” into a bilateral system where a 2C booking app and a 2B merchant-management backend mesh and run together.

meta.scopeValue: Product Planning · UX · UI & Branding · 2B Backend System

summary.label: PROJECT SUMMARY
summary.heading: Converging a vague market vision into a complete design blueprint for a two-sided product.
summary.body: This is a Taiwanese course-booking app modeled on ClassPass. The core design task was handling the essential challenge of a “two-sided product” — the barrier of getting 2C users to switch from their existing habits, and a 2B merchant backend complete enough that merchants are willing to entrust their operations to it. With no existing product spec, I independently completed the feature planning, information architecture, and the 2C app and brand-website design, <highlight>and reverse-engineered the complete 2B merchant-management backend from the front-end interface.</highlight>

background.label: 01 — BACKGROUND
background.heading: To take three different classes, you first have to add three official LINE accounts
background.body: Overseas, course-aggregation platforms connect thousands of venues through a single app; but this model never truly served Taiwanese users — and the client saw this gap and its potential.
background.calloutBody: To take a yoga class, a boxing class, and a kettlebell class in Taiwan, you have to add three official LINE accounts, remember three sets of booking rules, and read three different schedule formats. There’s nowhere to “see all the nearby classes you can take in one place” — the cost of choosing a class is indirectly pushed onto the user.
background.axisHeading: Course data is the axis between 2C and 2B
background.axisBody: For a two-sided platform to work, both sides must have a meshing, consistent understanding of “the same data” — every field a 2C user sees corresponds to a record a 2B merchant maintains in the backend.
background.demandDesc: People who want to find and book a class
background.axisCenterDesc: The same data shared by both sides
background.supplyDesc: Venues that want to grow their classes

axisRows.consumer: Discover nearby classes by location on the search/explore page
axisRows.merchant: Create and list/unlist courses in the backend

axisRows.consumer: Pick a time slot that works for them
axisRows.merchant: Set the schedule, bind coaches and venues

axisRows.consumer: Compare price and remaining spots, then decide
axisRows.merchant: Set capacity limits and course pricing

axisRows.consumer: Confirm the booking and complete payment
axisRows.merchant: View the booking roster; spots deduct in real time

axisRows.consumer: See cancellation and reschedule rules before booking
axisRows.merchant: Set refund/reschedule policies in one place

axisRows.consumer: Leave a review after the class, shaping the next decision
axisRows.merchant: Read rating feedback as a basis for operational improvement

background.opportunityTitle: Not just an app design problem — it’s the design of a two-sided system
background.opportunityBody: The real design challenge wasn’t building the booking feature; it was answering two opposite questions at once — why would a 2C user switch from their existing LINE habit? And why would a 2B merchant entrust their course operations to a new platform with no user base yet? If either side’s experience is off-balance, the platform won’t turn.

market.label: 02 — COMPETITORS & MARKET OPPORTUNITY
market.heading: A persistent market opportunity
market.body: Positioning this platform’s market situation requires seeing two things at once: the absence of international brands, and the footprints of local predecessors.
market.tableHeading: Two market signals pointing to the same conclusion
market.row3Intl: The model holds long-term in other countries
market.row3Local: People in Taiwan genuinely need this service
market.row4Intl: The gap is still there, with no incumbent to compete against
market.insightCaption: A vacuum exists, but the model is hard to scale — what this project had to solve wasn’t just the “feature problem,” but a two-sided platform’s “recruitment problem.”
market.cardTitle: The need is real, but the model is hard to scale
market.cardBody: International course-aggregation platforms (like ClassPass) serve thousands of cities worldwide, yet never entered the Taiwanese market. And as early as 2014, Taiwan saw inspired local attempts (such as 17Fit and KFit) — they proved the need genuinely exists, but none grew into a large-enough platform.

challenge.label: 03 — CORE DESIGN CHALLENGE
challenge.heading: A product facing both 2C and 2B at once
challenge.card1Title: Simple enough to be “worth replacing the existing habit”
challenge.card1Body: Users are already used to LINE or other ways of booking classes. To get them to switch, the new experience can’t just “also work” — it has to be noticeably less effort: see all the options in one place, complete a booking through a smoother flow. This converged into making “discover classes & book classes” the product’s core feature plan.
challenge.card2Title: Complete enough that “merchants are willing to hand over operations”
challenge.card2Body: The merchant backend serves venue owners who list and manage their own classes. The product must cover the merchant’s full operational workflow, and its logic must align with every field on the front end. With no PM spec, this entire system had to be derived independently and designed into reality.
challenge.asymHeading: The same product, two sides with nearly opposite design trade-offs
challenge.asymBody: The two cards above describe the nature of the two challenges — this table turns it into a quantifiable comparison, making the “asymmetry” visible.
challenge.col2cDesc: Remove everything unnecessary; leave the shortest path to a decision
challenge.col2bDesc: Fill in everything necessary to support the full operational flow

rows.label: Success criterion
rows.consumer: Whether it’s less effort than the existing LINE flow
rows.merchant: Whether it can replace the Excel and message-based reconciliation merchants use now

rows.label: Main scope
rows.merchant: 8+ operational modules: courses · schedule · venues · coaches · orders · cancel/reschedule · reviews · reports

rows.label: Unit of measure
rows.consumer: Speed and smoothness of the user experience
rows.merchant: Workflow completeness (every front-end field has a backend source)

rows.label: What failure looks like
rows.consumer: One extra tap, one extra thought → fall back to LINE
rows.merchant: One missing field, one missing action → fall back to reconciling in Excel

challenge.readingCaption: The 2C column should be as short as possible, the 2B column as complete as possible: in the same product, “doing it well” means two opposite things on the two sides.

process.label: 04 — 0~1 DESIGN PROCESS
process.heading: From a vague brief to an executable blueprint
process.body: The client brought a direction, not a spec. The core task of the design process was to converge it, step by step, into a product blueprint that could be handed off to engineering.
process.step1Body: Through interviews, I clarified the business goals and target audience, and defined the MVP scope against the ClassPass model — distinguishing “the minimum feature set that makes the platform turn” from “features that can wait for later iterations.”
process.step2Body: I drew wireframes to map out the feature flows and aligned on requirements with the client one by one. Here, the wireframe’s role wasn’t the screen but aligning language — making “the features the client describes” and “the interface to actually design” the same thing.
process.step3Body: I first proposed the product’s color and style direction; once the style was anchored, I designed the app home as the overall visual baseline before expanding to the rest of the interfaces.
process.step4Body: I held regular meetings with the client and engineers, dynamically adjusted design requirements, and handed off the design output to engineers for implementation.

app.label: 05 — DESIGN OUTPUT: 2C APP
app.heading: App UI & UX
app.body: The 2C app had a single design goal — make “finding and booking a class” noticeably less effort than the existing flow of “Google it yourself, add an official LINE to book.”
app.flowImgAlt: 2C app main flow scroll image: Discover → Book → Done
app.decisionsHeading: Walking with the user through every moment inside the app
app.decisionsBody: Below are a few key interface-design judgments from this project.
app.d1Moment: “I’ll have some free time soon — what can I take nearby?”
app.d1Title: The search/explore page organizes classes by “nearby”
app.d1Body: The real situation when a user opens the app is “I’ll have time soon, what’s nearby that I can take,” so the search/explore page organizes classes around location and category.
app.d2Title: Course cards carry only the info “needed to decide”
app.d2Body: Cards are filtered by the standard of “is it worth the user tapping in,” so they keep only the class name, duration, location, and rating; everything else is saved for the detail page.
app.d3Title: The cancellation policy is surfaced before “confirm booking”
app.d3Body: The biggest source of complaints in booking-type products is “I thought I could cancel.” Putting cancellation and reschedule rules before the confirm-booking step — rather than hiding them in a terms page — lets users understand the rules before they pay any cost.
app.d4Moment: “Every field on the front end is a design decision behind the scenes”
app.d4Title: The app backend is designed in sync with 2C
app.d4Body: Every dynamic field in the 2C app needs an input source behind it. The app backend was planned in sync with the front end to ensure front-end presentation and backend maintenance stay consistent — which also leads into the backend-system design in the next section.
app.img1Alt: App key screen 01: with design-decision annotations

web.label: 06 — BRAND WEBSITES
web.heading: Brand-website design facing both 2C & 2B
web.caption: Designing different content structures and visual tones for the two user types, so each page focuses on persuading just one kind of person — this is where a two-sided platform’s “recruiting both sides” lands at the brand layer.
web.img1Alt: 2C brand site: aimed at users looking for classes, leading with course variety, booking simplicity, and pricing flexibility
web.img2Alt: 2B brand site: aimed at venue merchants considering joining, leading with platform exposure and backend management

backend.label: 07 — DESIGN OUTPUT: 2B BACKEND SYSTEM
backend.heading: Every piece of information the front-end user sees is a designed input decision in the backend
backend.body: The 2B backend is a standalone system serving venue merchants who “manage their own classes.” With no existing spec, the entire backend’s content and structure was reverse-engineered all the way from the front end and defined independently. The 2C app and the 2B backend look like two products, but they are really two sides of the same data. Below is the method I used to derive the backend from scratch.
backend.method1Body: First, going screen by screen through the “front-end user scenario,” I inventoried which fields are variable and editable; then I switched to the “backend administrator scenario” to consider what information merchants need to see and operate on.
backend.method2Body: I grouped the inventoried features into the backend’s navigation structure; features needing special handling (e.g. content requiring review) became their own top-level category.
backend.method3Body: Under each top-level category, data is presented as lists. For special data displays (like charts), I traced back to ask “where does this number’s data come from” to ensure the backend can fetch it.
backend.method4Body: A list implies corresponding editable fields and create/edit/delete interfaces, so I designed the editing details of each object one by one.
backend.method5Body: I went back to the front-end interface and compared field by field, checking the backend for omissions — any front-end field without an input source in the backend is a hole.
backend.ifaceHeading: How a single course card decides what the backend looks like
backend.ifaceBody: Take the “course card” a user sees in the app: every one of its fields maps to a designed input in the backend.
backend.mapHeading: Course detail page → field mapping to the backend edit form
backend.mapColFront: Front end (shown on the 2C app course detail page)
backend.mapColBack: Backend (input in the 2B course edit form)
mapRows: Schedule planner: pick date and time slot

backend.img2Alt: Field-mapping diagram: front-end course card ↔ backend edit form

impact.label: 08 — Impact & Scope
impact.heading: The design scope delivered by one person
impact.body: Design delivery ends at “complete and ready to hand off to engineering.” Below it’s shown across two levels: design scope and experience change.
impact.metric1Sub: App · App backend · 2C web · 2B web · 2B backend
baRows: Add multiple venues’ official LINE accounts separately
See all nearby classes in one app
Three schedule formats, each looked up separately
Rules scattered, discovered only after the fact
Cancellation and reschedule policy stated up front, before booking
One 2B backend covering everything from listing to reconciliation
Every backend field maps to a front-end display, verified field by field

reflection.label: 09 — Reflection
reflection.heading: Given another chance, I’d move “validation” earlier next time
reflection.p1: This project let me fully experience designing a two-sided product from 0 to delivery. The biggest takeaway was the method of “reverse-engineering the backend system from the front end” — it later became my approach to front-/back-end feature-integration design.
reflection.p2: But if I did it again, there are two things I’d choose to do differently.
reflection.p3: The requirements this time came mainly from the client’s market observations, and within the project’s schedule constraints, there wasn’t enough time to research Taiwan’s existing competitor attempts more deeply. If I’d clarified earlier “why this business model didn’t seem to scale before,” the design could have responded sooner to the real risks — like the merchant cold-start that’s hardest for two-sided platforms — rather than just getting the features right.
reflection.sub2: “Plant measurable metrics for the design outcome”
reflection.p4: This delivery ended at “complete and ready to hand off to engineering,” missing post-launch data feedback. In the future I’ll define success metrics with the client during the design phase (e.g. booking-completion rate, time for merchants to list a course), so the design’s value can be validated, not just delivered.
reflection.p5: In a 0-to-1 project, the most valuable experience is often not making the interface pretty, but — when information is incomplete — still being able to break a vague vision into a system that meshes together and can be executed. This project gave me much more experience in front-/back-end feature-integration design.

projectStatus.label: Project Status —
projectStatus.body: The design was delivered and published to TestFlight for beta testing; due to contractual factors between the client and the company, the product did not reach official launch.
